result.summary: Pausanias discusses the founding and name of Psophis in Arcadia, its rivers and sanctuaries, and the tomb of Alcmæon. He tells Alcmæon's flight after killing his mother, his marriages and death, and adds remarks on river silt and on Aglaus.

scenes.title: Founding and sights of Psophis
scenes.summary: Pausanias gives rival accounts of who Psophis was, describes the rivers, the Erymanthian boar and the temple of Aphrodite Erycina.

scenes.title: Alcmæon at Psophis
scenes.summary: Alcmæon, mad after killing his mother, marries Alphesibœa, later weds Callirhoe and is killed by Phegeus' sons over the necklace.
scenes.stakes: Alcmæon is pursued by the Avenger of his mother's blood and finally loses his life.

scenes.title: Rivers, statues and Aglaus
scenes.summary: Pausanias compares river silting, describes the river-god's temple and doubts the tale of Aglaus's lifelong happiness.

alias_notes.explanation: The town's earlier name, formerly Erymanthus, before the sons of Hercules renamed it Psophis.
Aphrodite worshipped under the surname from Mount Eryx.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias' moralizing aside on foolish desire, introducing Callirhoe's fatal wish for the necklace.

analysis.text: Pausanias weighs competing local traditions and favors the one he finds most plausible, using geography and comparison to test myth.
The Alcmæon story shows Greek ideas of blood-guilt and pollution, and the use of delta formation as evidence for myth reflects Pausanias' rationalizing approach.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias notes that statues of the Nile were often made of black stone, unlike other river-gods' white stone.

language_notes.text: Sicania is an old name for Sicily, tied to the Sicani, its early inhabitants. Eryx was a legendary ruler there.
The text oddly makes Erymanthus a person, a hunter and lover, though it is a river; the river is spoken of as a mythic figure.
Cumæ in the Opic territory is the Greek colony in Campania, Italy, where the Opici lived. Pausanias doubts that such relics came from Greece.
Hero-chapels are small shrines where a dead hero received cult honours.
The famous necklace is the necklace of Harmonia, which Eriphyle accepted as a bribe to send her husband Amphiaraus to his death at Thebes.
The Avenger is the Fury pursuing a matricide. The oracle means he must find newly formed land, not yet existing when he committed the crime.
Silting means the deposit of river mud, here building new land at the Achelous's mouth.
The expedition against Thebes is the war of the Seven, in which Alcmæon later took part as an Epigonus, avenging his father.
Homer's jars of Zeus appear in the Iliad, Book 24, where Zeus gives mortals mixed gifts of good and evil.

context_notes.text: Capturing the Erymanthian boar was one of Hercules' twelve labours, set by his cousin King Eurystheus.
Aphrodite Erycina was worshipped at Mount Eryx in Sicily; her wealthy temple there was famous. Paphos in Cyprus was her other great shrine.
Callirhoe's wish for the necklace brings about Alcmæon's death, so the cursed heirloom keeps destroying its owners.
The Mæander is a winding river in Asia Minor. Priene and Miletus were once coastal cities, later left inland by silt.
Crœsus was the proverbially wealthy king of Lydia in the sixth century BC, linked in tradition with ideas of human happiness.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias weighs rival traditions and openly declares one 'truest', showing his habit of critical judgment over local legend.
Pausanias gently undercuts the Cumæans' proud relic by dismissing it as improbable, a mild skepticism typical of his tone.
The cypresses, called Maidens, serve as living memorials. They give the modest tomb a sacred, funereal dignity.
Pausanias interrupts the story with a moralizing aside, giving the myth a lesson about human folly.
Pausanias compares human lives to ships in storms to argue that no one avoids misfortune altogether.
